# Task 3: Impact of Human Genetic Variation on CRISPR Guide Performance

```{r}
#| label: task3-setup
#| include: false
# Paths are relative to this chapter, including when rendered in a Quarto book.
input_file <- knitr::current_input(dir = TRUE)
chapter_dir <- if (nzchar(input_file)) dirname(normalizePath(input_file)) else getwd()
read_task3 <- function(name) {
  read.csv(file.path(chapter_dir, "data", name), stringsAsFactors = FALSE,
           check.names = FALSE)
}
selected_guides <- c("200forw", "248forw")
samples <- c("HG00142", "HG00178", "HG00237", "HG01521",
             "HG03129", "NA19175", "NA19462")
# Original carrier export. Its Risk labels are not used in the corrected report.
hits <- read_task3("Task3_variant_hits.csv")
# Exact sequence pair and all seven genotypes transcribed from Task3.html.
site <- read_task3("Task3_site_snapshot.csv")
stopifnot(nrow(site) == 1L, all(samples %in% names(site)),
          all(hits$Guide %in% selected_guides),
          !anyDuplicated(hits[c("Guide", "Chromosome", "Position", "Sample")]))

split_gt <- function(gt) {
  alleles <- strsplit(gt, "[|/]")[[1L]]
  if (length(alleles) != 2L || any(!grepl("^[0-9]+$", alleles))) {
    return(c(NA_integer_, NA_integer_))
  }
  as.integer(alleles)
}
mm20 <- function(guide, target) {
  stopifnot(nchar(guide) == 23L, nchar(target) == 23L,
            grepl("^[ACGT]+$", guide), grepl("^[ACGT]+$", target))
  sum(strsplit(substr(guide, 1L, 20L), "")[[1L]] !=
      strsplit(substr(target, 1L, 20L), "")[[1L]])
}
pam <- function(sequence) substr(sequence, 21L, 23L)
reference_mm <- mm20(site$GuideSeq, site$OriginalOfftarget)
alternate_mm <- mm20(site$GuideSeq, site$ModifiedOfftarget)
reference_pam <- pam(site$OriginalOfftarget)
alternate_pam <- pam(site$ModifiedOfftarget)
stopifnot(reference_mm == site$OriginalMismatch,
          reference_mm == 4L, alternate_mm == 4L,
          reference_pam == "AGG", alternate_pam == "AGA",
          substr(site$OriginalOfftarget, 1L, 20L) ==
            substr(site$ModifiedOfftarget, 1L, 20L))

individual <- data.frame(Individual = samples,
  Genotype = vapply(samples, function(s) site[[s]][1L], character(1)),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
gt <- t(vapply(individual$Genotype, split_gt, integer(2)))
stopifnot(!anyNA(gt), all(gt %in% c(0L, 1L)))
individual$`Reference PAM copies` <- rowSums(gt == 0L)
individual$`Alternate PAM copies` <- rowSums(gt == 1L)
individual$`PAMs on the two haplotypes` <- vapply(seq_len(nrow(gt)),
  function(i) paste(ifelse(gt[i, ] == 0L, reference_pam, alternate_pam),
                   collapse = " / "), character(1))
carrier_samples <- individual$Individual[individual$`Alternate PAM copies` > 0L]
stopifnot(setequal(carrier_samples, hits$Sample),
          all(hits$Genotype == individual$Genotype[match(hits$Sample, samples)]),
          all(hits$Position == site$Position), all(hits$REF == site$REF),
          all(hits$ALT == site$ALT), all(hits$Chromosome == site$Chromosome))

unique_hits <- unique(hits[c("Guide", "Chromosome", "Position", "REF", "ALT")])
guide_summary <- data.frame(Guide = selected_guides,
  `Unique overlapping variants` = vapply(selected_guides,
    function(g) sum(unique_hits$Guide == g), integer(1)),
  `ALT carriers (out of 7)` = vapply(selected_guides,
    function(g) length(unique(hits$Sample[hits$Guide == g])), integer(1)),
  check.names = FALSE)
number_carriers <- length(carrier_samples)
number_heterozygous <- sum(individual$`Alternate PAM copies` == 1L)
number_homozygous_alt <- sum(individual$`Alternate PAM copies` == 2L)
number_reference <- sum(individual$`Alternate PAM copies` == 0L)
```

## Objective

In Task 2, two CRISPR interference (CRISPRi) guide RNAs, **200forw** and **248forw**, were selected to target the first exon of the **OAS2** gene based on predicted efficiency and specificity scores generated by CRISPOR [@haeussler2016]. Because these predictions are based on the human reference genome, naturally occurring genetic variation may alter guide RNA target regions or predicted off-target sites in individual genomes. This analysis therefore investigated whether variants present in seven human genomes affected guide availability or altered predicted off-target risk.

## Approach

The CRISPOR off-target prediction table generated in Task 2 was originally imported into a Python Jupyter Notebook and filtered to include only the selected OAS2 guides (200forw and 248forw). Predicted off-target coordinates, guide sequences, mismatch counts and off-target scores were extracted for further analysis. Reusing these predictions provided a direct way to refine the guide selection from Task 2, while keeping the same candidate guides.

Variant information was obtained from the chromosome 1 and chromosome 2 VCF files used in the original analysis. These datasets contained genomic variants and genotypes for seven individuals: HG00142, HG00178, HG00237, HG01521, HG03129, NA19175 and NA19462. A VCF records the reference and alternate alleles, their genomic positions and individual genotypes [@danecek2011]. Variant positions were compared with the predicted off-target intervals on these two chromosomes. Sites on other chromosomes were not assessed. This is a targeted reassessment of reference-predicted sites, rather than a new genome-wide off-target search.

For the single overlapping SNP, the original notebook recorded the reference and alternate off-target sequences. This R analysis separates each 23-base sequence into its **20-base protospacer** (the DNA sequence matched by the guide) and its **3-base PAM**. Mismatches are counted only within the protospacer; the PAM is assessed separately. This follows Lecture 6, which describes the canonical SpCas9 target as a 23-base sequence with an NGG PAM [@qutlecture6]. Mismatch counts alone cannot quantify off-target activity: mismatch position and type also matter for MIT and CFD scores[@haeussler2016].

The genotype was used to distinguish reference homozygotes, heterozygotes and alternate homozygotes. In the VCF, `0` denotes the reference allele, `1` the first alternate allele, and `|` indicates phased alleles [@danecek2011]. The original CRISPOR MIT and CFD scores were not recalculated and are not presented as scores for the alternate sequence.

**Data provenance and scope.** The supplied files contain the original HTML notebook and exported results, but not the original VCFs or the full CRISPOR table. The tables below are regenerated in R from the carrier CSV and a small snapshot transcribed from the displayed notebook output. The sequence comparisons and genotype interpretation are recalculated here; the original genome-wide inputs have not been independently rerun. The [Reproducibility chapter](reproducibility.qmd) describes how to repeat the chromosome 1/2 overlap analysis when those inputs are supplied. The original Task 3 report specifies GRCh38; the VCF assembly must be checked against the CRISPOR assembly before rerunning.

## Findings

### Guide Availability in Individual Genomes

The availability of the intended OAS2 target sequences **could not be established from this analysis**. OAS2 is located on chromosome 12, whereas the original VCF comparison used only chromosomes 1 and 2. Therefore, an absence of variants in the assessed off-target regions does not show that either intended target is unchanged in all seven individuals.

To answer this question, both intended 20-base target sequences and their PAMs must be checked at the exact OAS2 coordinates selected in Task 2 using matching chromosome 12 variant data. Until then, the on-target availability of both guides remains **not assessed**, and their suitability in each individual cannot be confirmed.

### Variants Affecting Predicted Off-Target Sites

Comparison of predicted off-target coordinates with the chromosome 1 and chromosome 2 VCF datasets identified a single variant overlapping a predicted off-target site associated with guide **248forw** (@tbl-task3-variant). The variant was a G to A substitution at chromosome 1 position **224,887,199**. It was present in `r number_carriers` individuals (HG00142, HG03129, NA19175 and NA19462), while the remaining `r number_reference` individuals carried the reference genotype at this position. No overlapping variants were reported for guide 200forw within the reference-predicted sites assessed on chromosomes 1 and 2.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-task3-variant
#| tbl-cap: "Variant identified within a reference-predicted off-target site."
variant_table <- data.frame(
  Guide = site$Guide,
  Chromosome = site$Chromosome,
  Position = format(site$Position, big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE),
  REF = site$REF, ALT = site$ALT,
  `ALT carriers` = paste0(number_carriers, "/", length(samples)),
  check.names = FALSE)
knitr::kable(variant_table)
```

There was **one unique overlapping variant in four individuals**, rather than four different variants. The guide-level results are summarised in @tbl-task3-summary.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-task3-summary
#| tbl-cap: "Summary of the original chromosome 1/2 off-target overlap results."
knitr::kable(guide_summary)
```

### Effect on Off-Target Binding Risk

The G to A substitution changes the PAM of the reported off-target sequence from **AGG to AGA** (@tbl-task3-sequences). It does **not** change the 20-base protospacer: its mismatch count remains **`r reference_mm` before and `r alternate_mm` after the variant**. Comparing all 23 bases would mix protospacer mismatches with PAM differences and would not be comparable with the original CRISPOR mismatch count.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-task3-sequences
#| tbl-cap: "Sequence comparison for guide 248forw. PAMs are assessed separately from protospacer mismatches."
sequence_table <- data.frame(
  Sequence = c("Guide target", "Reference off-target", "Alternate off-target"),
  `20-base protospacer` = c(substr(site$GuideSeq, 1, 20),
                            substr(site$OriginalOfftarget, 1, 20),
                            substr(site$ModifiedOfftarget, 1, 20)),
  PAM = c(pam(site$GuideSeq), reference_pam, alternate_pam),
  `Protospacer mismatches` = c(0L, reference_mm, alternate_mm),
  check.names = FALSE)
knitr::kable(sequence_table)
```

The alternate allele removes the canonical NGG PAM. Under the NGG-based framework used for guide selection, this makes the alternate sequence a less suitable off-target candidate. This is a qualitative prediction; it does not establish zero binding or a measured reduction in activity. Noncanonical PAMs can sometimes support Cas9 activity [@haeussler2016].

Individual-level analysis showed different effects depending on genotype (@tbl-task3-individuals). **`r number_heterozygous` individuals are heterozygous**: one haplotype has the altered AGA PAM, while the other retains the reference AGG PAM. **NA19462 is homozygous for the alternate allele**, so both haplotypes have the altered PAM. Consequently, all four carriers should not be assigned the same whole-individual reduction in risk. Allele copy counts do not imply a proportional change in binding.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-task3-individuals
#| tbl-cap: "Individual genotypes and PAMs at the variant-associated 248forw off-target site. PAM order follows the phased genotype."
knitr::kable(individual)
```

## Discussion

The results demonstrate that human genetic variation can influence CRISPR specificity predictions. A SNP within a predicted off-target site for guide 248forw changes its PAM, while the guide-complementary sequence retains four mismatches. The effect is allele-specific: three carriers retain a reference haplotype, whereas NA19462 carries the altered PAM on both haplotypes. These differences show why patient-specific genotypes should be considered when refining reference-based predictions. Previous work has also shown that human variants can create or remove PAMs and alter on-target and off-target specificity [@lessard2017].

However, the findings apply only to the reference-predicted off-target sites assessed with chromosome 1 and chromosome 2 data. No overlapping variant was reported for guide 200forw in this subset; this does not establish that its full specificity profile is unchanged. Variants elsewhere could create new off-target sites that were absent from the reference-based CRISPOR list. A more complete assessment would reconstruct individual haplotypes using matching reference and VCF data and repeat the off-target search, or use a variant-aware tool. The chromosome 12 on-target sites also need to be assessed before confirming guide availability in any individual.

Finally, this project uses **CRISPRi**, which regulates transcription using nuclease-deactivated Cas9 rather than cutting DNA [@jensen2021]. Therefore, these results concern potential off-target recognition and unintended gene regulation. CRISPOR cleavage-based scores do not directly measure CRISPRi repression. Experimental validation would be needed to confirm the functional effect of the PAM change.

## Conclusion

Analysis of the supplied results identified one SNP overlapping a reference-predicted off-target site for guide 248forw in four of seven individuals. The variant changes the PAM from AGG to AGA while leaving the protospacer mismatch count at four. Three carriers are heterozygous and retain one reference haplotype; NA19462 is homozygous for the alternate allele. No overlapping variant was reported for guide 200forw in the chromosome 1/2 subset. The intended OAS2 target sites were not assessed, so guide availability remains unresolved. Overall, these findings show that human genetic variation should be considered during guide evaluation, while a wider analysis is needed to confirm individual guide suitability.
